From the St Thomas Times, Aug. '23, 1848. The steamer from Southampton, via Bermuda with the 1st August mails, lias doubtless been detained bv the tempestuous weather we experienced yesterday. The gale com meneed at 1 1 a. m and threatened about an hour afterwards to become a perfect hurri cane. The inhabitants warned by the dis astrous visitation of 1837, and naturally alarmed set to work with energy to bar and secure their houses from t Ire fury of the expected tempest. Providentially however, at about 2 p m the storm lulled, and the wei come flashes of lightning, followed by the still more welcome peals of distant thunder dispelled all (ears «for the time being We are extremely happy to sav that no material injury Was infl cted on the stores or dwellings t slates, shingles, and tiles flew about, and a few old fences were laid flat : beyond this we have not heard of any casualty on shore in the harbour two or three boats Were upset, tiut uo lives were lost During the brief duration of the gale, the wind shift ed so often that we were unable to conjecture from wliat quarter it þÿ c a m e we Irusf it was only a local storm, and that none of the neighbouring islands have suffered. We regret to add that the French barque Packet de Charleston fiom Bordeaux went on shore outside the harbour near Green Key and it is feared will be a total wreck. She was lying on and oft' the harbor at the commencement of the galeþÿ captain, passengers, crew, all providentially saved. DENMARK ANI) THE D&UIUES,

An important notification has appeared in the London Official Gazette from which we make the following extracts :þÿ NOTIFICATION : IN RESPECT TO THE NUI- SANCES REMOVAL and diseases PREVEN- TION act. General Hoard of Health, Gwyder House October 5th 1848. The General Board of Health having considered the official accounts which have
been received of the course of the Asiatic cholera since the presentation of Ihc reports of the Metropolitan Sanitary Commissioners,

and having consulted medical pinctiiioneis of eminence and of special knowledge of the subject, and having þÿ c o m p a r t d the tenor of those recent accounts with the ohsei vations made respecting the former mode ot the propagation of Asiatic cholera in Cot ope have now to represent þÿ The chief predisposing causes of every epidemic, and especially of cholera, are damp, moisture, filth, animal and vegetable matters in a state of decomposition, nt:d in general whatever produces atmospheric imputin' ; all of which have the effect of lowering the health and vigour of the system, and of increasing the susceptibility to disease, particularly the young the aged at d the feeble. The attacks of cholera are uniformly found to he most frequent aud virulent in low Ling districts, on the banks of rivers, in the neighbouthood of sewer mouths, and wherever there are large þÿ c o l e c t i o n s of refuse, particularly amidst human dwellings. In a recent proclamation, issued for the protection of the population of the Russian empire, the important influence ol these and similar causes has been recognised, and the prarkjiuiLt-cTTintmendations founded thereon ar d vftTTrep the person and dwelling plaCe-Jifurfn, to allow of no sinks near the house, to admit of no poultry within the house, to keep every apartment as airy as possible by ventilation, and to prevent crowding wherever there ato þÿ s i c k . Next to the perfect cleansing of the premises, dryness ought to be carelully promo-

ted, which will of course require the keeping up of sufficient fues, particularly in damp and unhealthy districts. Medical authorities are agreed that the remedies proper for the premonitory symptoms are the same as those found efficacious in common diarrhae; that the most simple remedies will suffice, if given on the first manifestation of this symptom ; and that the following, which ore within the reach and management of every one, may be regarded as among the most þÿ u s e f u l namely, twenty grains of opiate confaet ion, mixed with two (able spoonsful of peppermint water, or with a little weak brandy and water, and repeated every three or four hours, or oftener, if the attack is severe, until the looseness of the bowels is slopped ; or an ounce of I he compound chalk mixture with ten or fifteen grains of the aromatic confection, and from five to ten drops of laudanum, repeated in the same manner. From half a drachm to a drachm of tincture of catechu may be added to this Iasi, if the attack is severe. Half these quantities should lie given to young persons under fifteen, and slili smaller doses for infants. It is recommended to repeat these remedies night and morning, tor some days after the looseness of the bowels has been stopped. But, in all cases, it is desirable, whenever practicable that even in this eat lies! stage of the disorder recourse should be had tr medical aid on the spot. Next in importance to the immediate employment of such remedies is attention to

proper diet and clothing. Whenever Asiatic cholera is epidemic, tiiere is invariably found among great numbers of the inhabitant an extraordinary tendency to irritation ol thu bowels, and this fact suggests, that QVetv article of food which is known to favour a relaxed stale of the bowels, should as far as pn«|ib!c, be þÿ a v o i d e d such as every variety

of green vegetables, whether cooked or not, ns cabbage, cucumber, and salad. It will be important also to abstain froth fiuits of all kinds, though ripe and even cooked, and whether diied or preserved. The most wholesome articles of vegetable diet þÿ a r e woll baked, but .not new bread, rice, oatmeal, and good potatoes. þÿ J i c k l e s should be avoided. Articles of food and drink whirl) in ordinary seasons, are generally wholesome, and agree well with the individual eonstitution, may, under this unusual condition, prove highly dangerous. The diet should be solid lather than fluid ; and those who have the means of choosing should live principally on animal food, as affording the most concentrated and invigorating diet ; avoiding salted and smoked meats, poik, sailed and shell fish, eider, perry, ginger beer, lemonu le, acid liquors of all descrip tions, and ardent spit its. Great moderation, both in food and drink, is absolutely essential to safety, during the whole duration of the epidemic period. One single act of indiscretion has, in many instances, been followed by a speedy and lata! attack. The intervals between the meals should not he long, cholera being uniformly-found to prevail with extraordinary intensity among the classes that observe the protracted fasts common in Eastern and some European countries. The practical importance of these cautions >r Adair Craw ford states, tbit in Russia the nught be illustrated by striking examples. m<»st intense of all t lie attacks weie those

that followed a hearty meal taken immediately after a protracted fast. In our own country, during its former visitation, the most frequent and deadly attacks wore observed to be those that look place in tbe middle of the þÿ n i k h t , a lew Irouis after a heavy supper. 'I be three fatal eases that have just occurred to sailers who have been at Hamburg, and who were brought sick to Hull turned out on inquiry to have followed very shortly alter the men had eaten a large quantity of plums, and had diunk freely of sum beer ; and the two still more recent fatal cases on board the ship Volant, of Sunderland, both occurred in drunkards, who persisted in the practice of intoxication, notwithstanding the earnest warnings that were given them against the dangers of intemperance. On account of the intimate connection between the external skin and the internal lining membrane of the bowels, warm clothing is of great importance. The wearing of flannels next the skin is therefore advisable. Recent experience on the continent seems to show, that it was useful to wear in the day tune a flannel bandage round the body, and tlris may become necessary in our own country during the damp and cold weather of the approaching season. þÿ l . n i i c o l a r attention should he paid to keeping the feet warm and dry ; changing the clothes immediately tiller exposure to wet ; and maintaining the sitting and Ltd rooms well aired, dry. and warm. It may he necessary to add a caution against the use of cold purgative medicines,

such as salts particular ly Glauber salts, and ieidlitz powders, which taken, in any quantity, in such a season, are danger. ms I b asin' purgatives of all kinds should be avoided such as senna, eoloev nth, and aloes, except trod-, i special medic.a I direction. Hags and Riches.þÿ One of those incidents which are so characteristic of the itinerant labourers from the Emerald Isle, who make their annual visit across the Channel at this season of the year, occurred last week on a farm in a neighbouring county. Along with a number of other persons, an Irishman was employed at the barley harvest during the day, and accommodated in the barn at night along with one of his fellow labourers. He was frequently in the habit of cautiously examining eei tain corners of his tattered gar mcnts as indicating that something of irn portance was concealed there On Monday week the sickles were busily at woik, and he had reached the end of his rig, and was about to whet the edge of his hook, when he was observed to become suddenly and alarmingly excited. He threw down first the sharpening stone, then his sickle, and the remnant of an old hat which protected his head from the burning sun. His hands were next busily employed in searching round the bottom of a vest which had evidently seen many harvests. At length, he exclaimed, ' It's gone, gone!" It was soon ascertained that a small bag, containing 11 sovereigns, which had been carefully sewed and pinned within the worn folds of his vest had escaped. All hands were quickly at work, in the hope of finding the lost bag, but their labours were in vain. Tiie character of General Cavaignac is still so imperfectly known to his own countrymen as well as to the rest of Europe, and the period has been so short which has claps ed since his translation from the inglorious labours of African warfare to the most ardu ous position which could be assigned to man in conducting the foreign and domestic trans actions of the French Republic, that we me disposed to watch with peculiar interest every indication of his opinions and his disposition. been wise Up and noble , they inspire respect to the present time they have and confidence ; and we are not surprised that some of the more eager contemporaries have already discovered the elements of a comparison between the policy and temper of the head of the French Government and the name of Washington We are not prepared to apply so exalted a standard of re publican merit at this stage of General (.'a þÿ v a i g n a o s career; hut we have as vet perceived in him nothing that is not sincere and honourable. We know that lie commands the good opinion, not only of the friends of republican institutions, but of their political antagonists ; he has shown a high courage without ambition, a resolute sense ol duly temoeied with great modesty, and a manliness of language which forbids the suspicion of disguise. These nre great qualities, anil if they hear the test of uncontrolled power and universal authority, General Cavaignac will have little to desire, unless it be a people not led astray by revolutionary theories

or military glories, hut willing to he tilled hv an honest, pacific, and manly government þÿ We are not ignorant that a large parly of the most zealous and enlightened fiiends of order in France view General þÿ U n v a i g n n c s policy with far more distrust and dissatisfaction than we entertain, or than they themselves publicly express. They impute to him a species of culpable toleration of that extreme party in the Republic: whose open aggressions on society he has resisted in the streets, and whose scandalous journals he has proscribed. They accuse him of a disposition to screnn from punishment, and from even the infamy of public exposure, men who, like Louis Hlane. and Cnussidierc. are open to the weigh tiest charges ; and they hold that his own predilection for republican institutions makes him indilFerent to the dangers to which they expose all that is valuable to the nation. We record these impressions of the lime without parncipaiing in them ; too little is known ns vet of Genuial Cavaignac to enable us to applaud or to censure him, and we are con tent to take the good we see in him, and leave him to lake care of his future fame. But happily, that which is most certainly known of him, and is more clear and explicit in his conduct, is his loreign policy, especially in the Italian question, and in t ho relations he has sought to establish with this country.þÿ On this ground he made, in answer to qtifis tions pul to him with reference to the Italian mediation the most important and successful

speech he has yet delivered, and he encountered with great superior itv an opponent far moie practised than himself in the war of words We have seldom read a more dexterous address, if, indeed, it had not higher merits than those of oratorical ingenuity,

s t v n o 2 :z A T 2 3 than this speech of the head of the Ftenrh government. Without affection he alludes to his own limited experience of the language of diplomacy and of deflate ; without hesitation, and in words as strong as those used by M. Guizot on a similar occasion, he declare his steadfast adherence to the cause of peace, and he repeats, " ns a thought which is ever present to þÿ h i m , his conviction that in a country like France more courage is needed to plead the Cause of peace than to counsel w ar. and that in his judgment the claims of statesmen who have waged that pacific combat stand higher than the fume of soldiers who have indulged the impulse of military ambition. To resume the sword for the defence of hist country would he to him no more than a return to the duties ol his entire lifeþÿ the higher duty is to keep it sheathed þÿ With these principles, and the detet initiation þÿ t o resist with unshaken fnmness all the impulses which may appear too prejudicial to the future destinies of the Republic," Ge nural Oavaignoc naturally resolved to interfere in Italy by pacific means alone, and to render those paciltc means effectual by seeking to act m concert with the British govern ment.

Strange Fish.þÿ Two fishermen, named Ross and Nichol from Larne, have now in their possession, in this town, a curious fish, which they intend to exhibit to the public this day in George's Market. It is of a very peculiar confirmation, the shape being nearly oval. It measures nearly live feet in length, and about three feet iri depth in the side, and weighs rather more than four cwt. The skin is very hard , and of a dark green hue, and on pressing it with thn finger feels as rough as the surface of a file. The head is very hard and thick, with a small projecting snout, beneath which is the mouthþÿ an aperture of about four inches in length by one and a half in breadth when open. It has no nostrils, and the eyes, which are not large, are situated in the upper part of the head.þÿ It has just but two fins, a dorsal and ventral, of a triangular shape about eighteen inches in length, and standing quite erect. The tail is of a most peculiar form, having five circular or rather elipiica! indentations, they being granulated ami nearly as hard as the upper pa rt of the body, and somewhat resembling a lady 's frill. The fishermen don't know the name of the fish, having never seen any thing of the same species before, but they state that an old seaman who examined it gave it the name of " Devil Fish" It was taken on Thursday evening, about four o'clock, at a place called Hunter's Buoy, a short distance from the " Maidens." It was observed floating lav ly on the suiface 'of the water, and suffered the boat to approach it

very closely. One of the men having in his hand what is called a "clip." to which was a small piece of rope, struck it on the back, and it then darted away with great fury, never attempting to go underneath the water. It look the boat a run of about three miles, and having been nearly exhausted as they thought, they managed to throw another rope about it, and then hauled it into the boat with great difficulty. When in the boat it nearly broke the sides in its struggle to get free, which were so great that two of the fishermen became alarmed and would very gladly have launched it overboard again into tfie sea. They succeeded, however, in killing it, by striking repeatedly with the "clip," and brought it into Belfast, where it now may be seen by those who are anv way curious in iehlhynburieal monsters. After exhibition the fishermen propose selling it.þÿ Belfast Paper. Whose wearisome and wild eareer, Like thine, is hounded to a span : it seems bot as a little day Since nature smil'd upon thy birth, And spring came forth in fair array, To dance upon thy joyous earth. Vet lovely in thy lifclessness, As beauty stretched upon the bier in death's clay cold and dark caress ; There's loveliness in thy decay, Which breathes, which lingers round thee still Like memory's mild and cheering ray, Beaming upon the night of ill. Yetþÿ yet the radiance is not gone Which shed a richness o'er the scene, Which smil'd upon the golden dawn When skies were biilliant and serene : Oh ! stifl a melancholy smile Gleams upon nature's aspect fair, To charm the eye a little while, Ere ruin spreads his mantle there ! Thou desolate and dying year ! Since Time entwin'd thy vernal wreath, How often Love hath shed the tear, And knelt beside ihe bed of death: H«,w many hearts, that lightly sprung Whenjov was blooming but to die, Their finest chords fry death unstrung, Have yielded life's expiring s gh. The arrival of the Steamer Trent bringing accounts lo the )7tlt ultimo, enables us to give a partial outline of affairs in Europe:þÿ In Franee every thing at present is tranquil. Marast on the 3rd November was elected as President of the National Assembly; on the following day the New Constitution was definitely voted, and on the 12th it was solemnly inaugurated bv religious ceremonies. On the 1st day of November, the whole of Vienna was in possession of the Imperial Troopsþÿ after a siege of eight davs. The German Parliament has passed, by immense majorities, two important sections of the New German Constitution. The first of these sections declares that no part of the German etnpiie can form one state with non Germanic countries; and the second enacts, that if a German country is under the rule of the same Sovereign with a non-Germanic, the relations of the two countries are to be settled according to the principles of a mere personal union It remains to be seen in what manner it will be attempted to apply these enactments to the Austrian empire, which they would throw into inextricable confusion. The Deputies of the Frankfort Assembly t» the Imperial Government had been arrested at Vienna. Ala tiers in Prussia tend to an alarming crisis as the appointment of Count Brandenburg as President arid minister of foreign Alfaris places the Monarch and the Chamber dirccilv at issue.þÿ General W range! had enicicd Berlin with a large force which on the 12th was declared

by royal decree to he in a state of siege for two miles in its circumference All clubs and political societies are dissolved. No person is allowed to carry arms. All public meetings are prohibited. In Denmark large forces still are assembling in Jutland arid other preparations are on foot evincing a determination to abide by their claim to the Duchies. The German and Danish Commissioners Stedman and lieedi/. had arrived . nexpec.tedlv at Copenhagen: the new Government Commission having greatly transgressed the limits of its lawful competency, as Count Ivmith said, perfectly justified M. lieedt/. in so doing. The Minister viewed the adhesion of the German to the Danish Government Commissioner as a favourable sign, meanwhile the enthusiasm in Denmark for their righteous cause continues on the increase ; petitions innumerable pour in day hv day praying that an end he >ut lo the present state of things, as the stipulations in the late armistice had not been fulfilled except by Denmark. VVe cannot therefore otherwise than suppose the war with Germany, etc long, will be vigorously renewed, and thence spread throughout Europe.

On Sunday. the 2!)th October. the Clmrr.h of St. Sidwell, in the city of Exeter, was the scene of a disgraceful riot doting the lime of the evening service, in consequence of the llev. J. Ingle, who officiated at the lecture, entering the pulpit in his surplice. It appears that Mr. Ingle, who is a young man, has persisted in this practice, notwithstanding the dislike of the parishioners to such proceedings, and notwithstanding the pastoral directions of the Bishop of the diocese some time hack, in consequence of the scenes which arose in tit Sidwell's and other churches from its adoption. The uproar commenced w ith a general "coughing down" (Several persons then moved towards the door, making a great noise in their progress ; a young woman went oil in a (it of hysterics, uttering loud shrieks, whilst a mob outside besieged the doors of the building. A cry of " Eire 1" was raised, followed by an announcement that the church doors were closed, and a rush was made to hurst them open. Some persons Fried, ' Turn him out!" " l'ut out his lights I" In the galleries the uproar was at its height, whistling the noise of catcalls, and such cries as ate heard in theatres, hurrahing, &c., echoed throughout the edifice. Mr. Ingle still persisted to read his text, but was quite inaudible, and the row increased, some of the congregations waving their hats, standing on lite seats, jumping over the seats, bawling, roaring, ami gesticulating, like a mob at an elec-

tion The rev. gentleman, in the midst of the confusion, despatched a message to lite mayor respecting his assistance, and whi st the messenger was gone on his errand the church warden, Mr. llavntnn. .addressed the people, and also n quested Mr logic to te move the cause of the ill feeling < xptessed at his appearance. Mr. Ingle Heated the te quest with indifference, upon which a Mr. B llili addressed him in no measured let ins, and insisted on his leaving the pulpit. The mayor at length arrived, and shortly afterwards the superintendent of the police and several constables. The llev. Chancellor Harrington and the Venerable Archdeacon Bartholomew also arrived. The mayor enforced silence, and after admonishing the people, requested the clergyman to leave the pulpit for a few minutes, and to speak to him in the vestry. Mr. Ingle treated the mayor's request with the same disrespect he had the other remonstrances addressed to him. He refuseit to comply, and took advantage of the temporary lull to give out his text and proceed with his discourse, the matter of which was supplied from the recent political events in Buns and Ireland. At its conclusion he declined the advice of the mayor to retiie to his home by a private way into Longbrookstreet. Further evils were, however, avertcd by his friends carrying him off by the way the mayor proposed. The damage done to the interior of thu church is said to be very considerable.
